Legality means the state or quality of being allowed, permitted, or valid according to the law.

When something has legality, it means the law allows it to exist or happen. When something lacks legality, the law forbids it.

Think of the law as a giant rulebook that a society follows. Legality is simply the question: "Does this rulebook permit this thing?" If yes — it has legality. If no — it lacks legality.

The word works as an answer to the question: "Is this legal?"

  • Driving a car on a public road → has legality (the law permits it, provided you follow the rules)
  • Stealing from a shop → lacks legality (the law forbids it)

So "legality" is not a thing you can touch or see. It is a status — a quality that an action, an object, a contract, a transaction, or a situation either has or doesn't have, depending on what the law says about it.
Legality Is Not the Same as Morality

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word.

Legal ≠ Good. Illegal ≠ Bad.

Something can be legal but still morally wrong. Historically, slavery was legal in many countries — it had legality — but it was deeply immoral. Something can also be illegal but morally justifiable, like hiding innocent people from a violent government.

So legality is purely about what the law says, not about what is right or wrong in a deeper human sense. The law and morality often overlap, but they are not the same thing.
Legality Depends on Place and Time

Here is another crucial point: legality is not universal or permanent. It shifts based on where you are and when you are.

  • Gambling might be fully legal in one country and completely banned in the neighboring one.
  • Consuming certain substances was illegal decades ago in a country but is perfectly legal there today.
  • A contract that was valid and legal under old laws might lose its legality when new laws are passed.

This means legality is always contextual — tied to a specific legal system, in a specific place, at a specific time.

When used in the plural — legalities — the word shifts slightly in meaning. It refers to the specific legal rules, requirements, or technicalities involved in a situation.

For example: "Before signing the contract, we need to go through all the legalities." This means: the specific legal formalities and requirements that must be checked or completed.

Or: "The deal fell apart because of legalities." Here it means legal complications or technical issues with the law got in the way.

So the singular ("legality") talks about the general status of whether something is legal. The plural ("legalities") talks about the specific legal rules and technical details at play in a situation.

Legality isn't always a clean yes-or-no answer. In real life, people often talk about it in degrees or with uncertainty:

  • Clear legality — something the law openly and explicitly allows, with no doubt.
  • Questionable legality — something that sits in a grey area, where it's not entirely clear whether the law permits or forbids it.
  • Doubtful legality — something that looks likely to be illegal but hasn't been tested or ruled on clearly.
  • No legality / illegality — something the law clearly forbids.

You'll often hear phrases like "the legality of this practice is disputed" — meaning lawyers and courts disagree on whether the law permits it or not.

These two words are close but different.

Legality = permitted by the written law.
Legitimacy = accepted as right, fair, or just — often by society, tradition, or moral standards.

A government might pass a law that is technically legal by its own constitution, but many people might argue it lacks legitimacy because it's unfair or unjust. The two concepts often go together, but not always.

Here are natural sentences showing how the word is used:

  • "The legality of the search was challenged in court." — Whether the search was permitted by law was disputed.
  • "No one questioned the legality of the transaction." — Everyone accepted that the transaction was lawful.
  • "The legality of the new regulation remains unclear." — It's uncertain whether the regulation is within what the law allows.
  • "They proceeded without checking the legality of their actions." — They acted without verifying whether the law permitted what they were doing.
  • "His legality as a citizen was confirmed." — His lawful status as a citizen was verified. (Less common, but used in immigration/legal status contexts.)

Legality is the quality or condition of something being in accordance with the law — meaning the law allows it, recognizes it, or validates it. It is a status, not a physical thing. It varies by country, region, and time period. It is separate from morality. In the plural, legalities refers to the specific legal rules or technical requirements involved in a situation. Understanding legality is essentially asking: "What does the law have to say about this?"
